chunks.text: This section is called Use answer information, then check independently. Use answer options as additional information when they are available, while still checking the original conditions. An option can be substituted or eliminated, but recognising a familiar-looking number is not evidence. For a numerical-response question, read the exact requested output. You may have found an intermediate digit, probability, count or measurement and still need one final operation to answer the question. Check in a way that attacks a different possible error. Substitute a candidate into every equation.

Compare a direct count with a complement. Check an optimum by separating its bound from its witness. Recompute a total from disjoint parts instead of repeating the same sequence of additions. A130 and A150 are useful for checking that a candidate satisfies every condition, including restrictions that were not used in the final arithmetic. Before moving on, open your notebook. chunks.text: Here is a worked teaching example for Choose a strategy, then learn from the decision. Use the larger number to organise a count Choose two different numbers from {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. Order does not matter. How many choices have a sum of at least 9? Use a complete classification, then check by a different count. Use only cells with smaller < larger. The four highlighted cells include both pairs summing exactly to 9, so the threshold is handled correctly. Work through the example 1.

Call the smaller number a and the larger number b, so a < b. This convention prevents counting a reversed pair twice. 2. If b ≤ 4, even the two largest possible numbers are 3 and 4, whose sum is 7. No such pair qualifies. 3. If b = 5, then a + 5 ≥ 9 forces a = 4, giving (4, 5). If b = 6, then a ≥ 3 gives (3, 6), (4, 6) and (5, 6). The count is 1 + 3 = 4. 4.

For an independent complement check, there are 6  times  5  divided by  2 = 15 unordered pairs altogether. Of the pairs with sum at most 8, 5 have smaller number 1, 4 have smaller number 2, and 2 have smaller number 3; there are no others. That is 11 pairs. 5. The complement gives 15 - 11 = 4, agreeing with the direct classification. Both methods include sum 9, because “at least 9” includes the boundary. Answer. 4 choices: {3, 6}, {4, 5}, {4, 6} and {5, 6}.

Here is the problem. Each pass through a machine doubles its input and then adds 3. Its output becomes the input for the next pass. Starting from a whole number x, find a formula for the output after n passes, for every integer n ≥ 0. Prove that your formula always works. Before calculating, say exactly what must be found or proved. Keep every restriction visible, because this is the kind of problem where a correct calculation can still answer the wrong question.

Editorial guidance: a common danger in a problem with this structure is this. A numerical pattern or checked example is evidence, but the question needs an argument that covers every allowed case. A useful first hint from the textbook is: Look for a fixed amount that you can add to each value so that one pass becomes simple multiplication. If you still need another nudge: Compare the new value plus 3 with the old value plus 3. Now work through the complete solution in small steps.

Pause whenever you want to reproduce a diagram, calculation or proof sentence in your notebook. Step 1. Let the current number be u and consider u + 3. After one pass, the new number plus 3 is (2u + 3) + 3 = 2(u + 3). Thus the shifted quantity doubles at every pass. Step 2. Starting from x, the initial shifted quantity is x + 3. After n passes it is 2n(x + 3), so the actual output is 2n(x + 3) - 3. Step 3.

For n = 0, the formula gives x, as required before any pass. If it gives the correct value after n passes, one more pass produces 2[2n(x + 3) - 3] + 3 = 2n + 1(x + 3) - 3. This proves the formula for every nonnegative integer n. The textbook answer is: 2n(x + 3) - 3. Return to the original problem. title: Triangles from two rows of points

chunks.text: Here is the problem. There are five distinct points on one horizontal line and four distinct points on a different parallel line. A triangle uses three non-collinear points. (a) Count all possible triangles whose vertices are chosen from these points. (b) Give a second method and explain why both methods count each triangle once. (c) Write a rule for m points on one line and n points on the other. Before calculating, say exactly what must be found or proved.

Keep every restriction visible, because this is the kind of problem where a correct calculation can still answer the wrong question. Editorial guidance: a common danger in a problem with this structure is this. A long list can miss a case or count the same object twice. Define one outcome and explain why the cases are complete and non-overlapping. A useful first hint from the textbook is: Decide which row supplies two of the three vertices.

If you still need another nudge: For another method, begin with all triples and remove exactly the collinear ones. Now work through the complete solution in small steps. Pause whenever you want to reproduce a diagram, calculation or proof sentence in your notebook. Step 1. (a) Every triangle has two vertices in one row and one in the other. Choosing two of the five upper points and one of the four lower points gives C(5, 2)  times  4 = 10  times  4 = 40 triangles.

Choosing two lower points and one upper point gives C(4, 2)  times  5 = 6  times  5 = 30. The total is 70. Step 2. These cases are disjoint: a triangle has exactly one row supplying its pair of vertices. They are complete because using all three vertices in one row gives a straight line, not a triangle. A line different from either row can meet each parallel row in at most one point, so a cross-row triple is never collinear.

Step 3. (b) Alternatively, choose any three of the nine points: C(9, 3) = 84 choices. Subtract the C(5, 3) = 10 triples wholly in the upper row and the C(4, 3) = 4 triples wholly in the lower row. These are exactly the collinear triples, leaving 84 - 10 - 4 = 70. Step 4. (c) The first method gives C(m, 2)n + C(n, 2)m = m(m - 1)n/2 + n(n - 1)m/2 = mn(m + n - 2)/2.

Here C(a, b) denotes the number of ways to choose b objects from a, without ordering them. The textbook answer is: (a) 70. (b) C(9, 3) - C(5, 3) - C(4, 3) = 70. (c) C(m, 2)n + C(n, 2)m = mn(m + n - 2)/2. Return to the original problem. title: A survey and its sharp overlap bounds

chunks.text: Here is the problem. In a class of 40, 24 play cricket and 21 play football. Seven play neither. (a) How many play both sports? How many play exactly one? (b) Draw a region diagram with all four counts. (c) Keeping 24 cricket players and 21 football players in a class of 40, find the smallest and largest possible overlap. Give an example of each. Before calculating, say exactly what must be found or proved.

Keep every restriction visible, because this is the kind of problem where a correct calculation can still answer the wrong question. Editorial guidance: a common danger in a problem with this structure is this. Finding one promising example is not enough. Keep the proof of the bound separate from the construction that reaches it. A useful first hint from the textbook is: First count the children in at least one sport.

If you still need another nudge: For part (c), a union cannot exceed the class and an overlap cannot exceed either sport. Now work through the complete solution in small steps. Pause whenever you want to reproduce a diagram, calculation or proof sentence in your notebook. Step 1. (a) The number playing at least one sport is 40 - 7 = 33. Adding the sport totals gives 24 + 21 = 45, but each child playing both was counted twice. The overlap is therefore 45 - 33 = 12.

Exactly one sport means at least one but not both, so 33 - 12 = 21. Step 2. (b) Cricket only is 24 - 12 = 12; both is 12; football only is 21 - 12 = 9; neither is 7. The four disjoint regions sum to 12 + 12 + 9 + 7 = 40. The cricket regions sum to 24 and the football regions to 21. The supplied region model shows all four counts. Step 3. (c) Now the number playing neither may change, while the class and the two sport totals remain fixed.

If the overlap is x, the union is 45 - x, which cannot exceed 40. Hence x ≥ 5. Also x cannot exceed the smaller sport total, so x ≤ 21. Step 4. Both bounds are attainable. For x = 5, the four counts (cricket only, both, football only, neither) are (19, 5, 16, 0). For x = 21, they are (3, 21, 0, 16). Each set of counts is nonnegative and gives the required class and sport totals.

More generally, any integer x between 5 and 21 produces the valid four counts (24 - x, x, 21 - x, x - 5), so there are no gaps between the extremes. The textbook answer is: (a) 12 play both; 21 play exactly one. (b) Cricket only 12, both 12, football only 9, neither 7. (c) Minimum overlap 5; maximum 21. Return to the original problem.

title: A cuboid painted on five faces

chunks.text: Here is the problem. A block is 3 unit cubes high, 4 wide and 5 deep. Its top and all four side faces are painted, but its bottom is not. (a) How many small cubes have at least one painted face? (b) How many have exactly three painted faces? How many have exactly two? (c) Find the numbers with exactly one and with zero painted faces, and check the grand total. Before calculating, say exactly what must be found or proved.

Keep every restriction visible, because this is the kind of problem where a correct calculation can still answer the wrong question. Editorial guidance: a common danger in a problem with this structure is this. A long list can miss a case or count the same object twice. Define one outcome and explain why the cases are complete and non-overlapping. A useful first hint from the textbook is: For at least one painted face, first count the cubes with no paint.

If you still need another nudge: Separate the top layer from the layers below it: the bottom face contributes no paint. Now work through the complete solution in small steps. Pause whenever you want to reproduce a diagram, calculation or proof sentence in your notebook. Step 1. There are 3  times  4  times  5 = 60 unit cubes. It is essential that the bottom is unpainted: a bottom-edge cube can have fewer painted faces than the corresponding top-edge cube.

Step 2. (a) A cube with no paint must avoid the left and right sides, front and back sides, and top. There are 4 - 2 = 2 interior width positions, 5 - 2 = 3 interior depth positions and 3 - 1 = 2 levels below the top. Thus 2  times  3  times  2 = 12 cubes are unpainted, leaving 60 - 12 = 48 with some paint. Step 3. (b) Exactly three painted faces occur at the four top corners.

For exactly two, first count the interiors of the top edges: 2(4 - 2) + 2(5 - 2) = 10. Then count the four vertical corner columns below the top: 4(3 - 1) = 8. These disjoint cases give 18. Step 4. (c) Exactly one painted face occurs at the (4 - 2)(5 - 2) = 6 top-face interior cubes and at 2[(4 - 2) + (5 - 2)](3 - 1) = 20 side-face interior cubes below the top. Hence there are 26. The classification checks: 12 + 26 + 18 + 4 = 60, and 26 + 18 + 4 = 48.

The textbook answer is: (a) 48. (b) Exactly three: 4; exactly two: 18. (c) Exactly one: 26; zero: 12. Total: 60. Return to the original problem. title: Choosing a bag and then a counter

chunks.text: Here is the problem. Bag A has 1 red and 3 blue counters. Bag B has 4 red and 2 blue. Bag A is chosen with probability 2/3 and bag B with probability 1/3; then a counter is drawn uniformly from that bag. Find the probability of red. What bag-choice probabilities would instead make all ten individual counters equally likely? Before calculating, say exactly what must be found or proved.

Keep every restriction visible, because this is the kind of problem where a correct calculation can still answer the wrong question. Editorial guidance: a common danger in a problem with this structure is this. Do not assume outcomes are equally likely until the random process has justified that sample space. A useful first hint from the textbook is: Multiply along each route: choose a bag, then choose a counter. If you still need another nudge: For equal individual likelihood, compare one named A counter with one named B counter.

Now work through the complete solution in small steps. Pause whenever you want to reproduce a diagram, calculation or proof sentence in your notebook. Step 1. Red can be obtained through two disjoint routes. Through A, its probability is (2/3)(1/4) = 1/6. Through B, it is (1/3)(4/6) = 2/9. Add these route probabilities: 1/6 + 2/9 = 3/18 + 4/18 = 7/18. Step 2. For the second part, let p be the probability of choosing A.

Any particular counter in A then has probability p/4. Any particular counter in B has probability (1 - p)/6. Equal likelihood requires p/4 = (1 - p)/6, hence 6p = 4 - 4p, so p = 2/5. Step 3. Thus choose A with probability 2/5 and B with probability 3/5. Every A counter then has probability (2/5)/4 = 1/10, and every B counter has probability (3/5)/6 = 1/10. This checks all ten individual outcomes and proves the choice is unique. Step 4.

Pooling the bags would give a red probability 5/10 = 1/2. That agrees with the newly calibrated bag choices, but not with the originally specified choices, whose red probability is 7/18. The textbook answer is: Probability of red: 7/18. To make each individual counter equally likely, choose A with probability 2/5 and B with probability 3/5. Return to the original problem.

title: Distinct digits on a full-day clock

chunks.text: Here is the problem. A 24-hour digital clock shows times from 00: 00 to 23: 59. For how many of these 1440 times are all four digits different? Before calculating, say exactly what must be found or proved. Keep every restriction visible, because this is the kind of problem where a correct calculation can still answer the wrong question. Editorial guidance: a common danger in a problem with this structure is this. A long list can miss a case or count the same object twice.

Define one outcome and explain why the cases are complete and non-overlapping. A useful first hint from the textbook is: Reject hours whose own digits repeat before counting any minutes. If you still need another nudge: The number of minute-tens choices depends on whether one or both hour digits lie between 0 and 5. Now work through the complete solution in small steps. Pause whenever you want to reproduce a diagram, calculation or proof sentence in your notebook. Step 1.

The two hour digits must first be different, so discard hours 00, 11 and 22. For each remaining hour, the minute tens digit must lie in {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and avoid both hour digits. The minute units digit must avoid the three digits already used, giving seven choices. Step 2. There are thirteen permissible hours whose two digits both lie in {0, …, 5}: 01, 02, 03, 04, 05, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 20, 21 and 23.

For each, four minute-tens digits remain and then seven minute-units digits, giving 4  times  7 = 28 times. Step 3. The remaining eight permissible hours are 06, 07, 08, 09, 16, 17, 18 and 19. Only one hour digit lies in the minute-tens set, so there are five minute-tens choices and seven units choices, giving 35 times per hour. Step 4. These disjoint cases cover every hour from 00 to 23. The total is 13  times  28 + 8  times  35 = 364 + 280 = 644. The textbook answer is: 644 times.

Return to the original problem. Check that every condition has been used, every counted case appears once, and any claimed maximum, minimum or guarantee has actually been proved rather than guessed from examples.

title: The smallest number with twelve divisors

chunks.text: Here is the problem. Count positive factors, including 1 and the number itself. (a) Check that 60 has twelve positive factors. (b) List the possible prime-exponent shapes of a number with twelve factors. (c) Use those shapes to prove that 60 is the smallest such number. Before calculating, say exactly what must be found or proved. Keep every restriction visible, because this is the kind of problem where a correct calculation can still answer the wrong question. Editorial guidance: a common danger in a problem with this structure is this.

Finding one promising example is not enough. Keep the proof of the bound separate from the construction that reaches it. A useful first hint from the textbook is: Explain why a prime exponent e gives e + 1 choices in a divisor. If you still need another nudge: Factor 12 in every unordered way using factors at least 2, then minimise each resulting prime-power shape. Now work through the complete solution in small steps. Pause whenever you want to reproduce a diagram, calculation or proof sentence in your notebook.

Step 1. (a) The twelve positive divisors of 60 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30, 60. Equivalently, 60 = 22  times  3  times  5, so the divisor count is (2 + 1)(1 + 1)(1 + 1) = 12. e₁ eᵣ Step 2. (b) If a number has prime factorisation p₁ … pᵣ , a divisor chooses an exponent from 0 to eᵢ independently for each prime. Its number of divisors is therefore (e₁ + 1) … (eᵣ + 1). Step 3.

The unordered factorizations of 12 into factors at least 2 are 12; 6  times  2; 4  times  3; and 3  times  2  times  2. Subtracting 1 from each factor gives the exponent shapes 11; (5, 1); (3, 2); and (2, 1, 1). Hence the four prime shapes listed in the answer are complete. Step 4. (c) For any fixed exponent shape, choose the smallest available primes.

Assign larger exponents to smaller primes: if p < q and a > b, then pa qb < pb qa because the ratio is (p/q)a - b < 1. Step 5. The smallest numbers for the four shapes are 211 = 2048; 25  times  3 = 96; 23  times  32 = 72; and 22  times  3  times  5 = 60. Every integer with twelve divisors has one of these shapes, and none can be smaller than its shape minimum. The smallest of the four minima is 60, which part (a) attains. The textbook answer is: 60.

The possible shapes are p11, p5q, p3q2 and p2qr, with distinct primes in each shape. Return to the original problem. Check that every condition has been used, every counted case appears once, and any claimed maximum, minimum or guarantee has actually been proved rather than guessed from examples.

title: Every labelled box must be used

chunks.text: Here is the problem. Five different badges are placed into three labelled boxes. Every box must receive at least one badge. How many assignments are possible? Before calculating, say exactly what must be found or proved. Keep every restriction visible, because this is the kind of problem where a correct calculation can still answer the wrong question. Editorial guidance: a common danger in a problem with this structure is this. A long list can miss a case or count the same object twice.

Define one outcome and explain why the cases are complete and non-overlapping. A useful first hint from the textbook is: Count all assignments before imposing the requirement that every box be used. If you still need another nudge: If only one box receives badges, how often does subtracting an empty-box case remove that assignment? Now work through the complete solution in small steps. Pause whenever you want to reproduce a diagram, calculation or proof sentence in your notebook. Step 1.

Without the nonempty restriction, each of the five distinct badges independently chooses one of three labelled boxes, giving 35 = 243 assignments. Step 2. For any specified empty box, all badges must lie in the other two boxes, giving 25 = 32 assignments. Subtracting for each of the three possible empty boxes gives 243 - 3  times  32. Step 3. However, an assignment using only one box has two empty boxes, so it was subtracted twice. There are three such assignments, one for each occupied box. Add each back once.

An assignment cannot have all three boxes empty because five badges must be placed. Step 4. Thus the number using all three boxes is 35 - 3  times  25 + 3 = 243 - 96 + 3 = 150. The subtraction removes every forbidden assignment exactly once overall. The textbook answer is: 150. Return to the original problem. title: Two different meanings of a random route

chunks.text: Here is the problem. A robot starts at (0, 0) and finishes at (2, 2), using only moves one unit right or one unit up and staying inside 0 ≤ x, y ≤ 2. At each step it chooses equally among its legal right/up moves; a boundary move may be forced. What is the probability that it visits (1, 1)? Compare this with choosing one of the six complete shortest routes uniformly. Before calculating, say exactly what must be found or proved.

Keep every restriction visible, because this is the kind of problem where a correct calculation can still answer the wrong question. Editorial guidance: a common danger in a problem with this structure is this. Do not assume outcomes are equally likely until the random process has justified that sample space. A useful first hint from the textbook is: A visit to (1, 1) is determined by the first two moves. If you still need another nudge: Check whether RRUU and RURU have the same probability under successive coin-flip choices.

Now work through the complete solution in small steps. Pause whenever you want to reproduce a diagram, calculation or proof sentence in your notebook. Step 1. The point (1, 1) is reached after exactly two moves. The first two moves must therefore be RU or UR. Under stepwise sampling, both moves in either of these prefixes occur where two choices are legal. Each prefix has probability (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4, so the probability of visiting (1, 1) is 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2. Step 2.

Under uniform complete-route sampling, the six possible strings are RRUU, RURU, RUUR, URRU, URUR and UURR. The four middle strings pass through (1, 1), so the probability is 4/6 = 2/3. Step 3. The experiments differ because forced boundary steps make complete strings unequally likely in the stepwise model. RRUU and UURR each have probability 1/4: after two identical moves, the remaining moves are forced. Each of the other four routes has probability 1/8.

Their probabilities sum to 2(1/4) + 4(1/8) = 1, and the four visiting routes total 1/2. The textbook answer is: Stepwise choices: 1/2. Uniform choice of a complete route: 2/3. Return to the original problem. title: A red counter and its hidden companion

chunks.text: Here is the problem. Three boxes contain two red counters, one red and one blue counter, and two blue counters, respectively. A box is chosen uniformly, then one of its two counters uniformly. Given that the drawn counter is red, what is the probability that the other counter in the chosen box is also red? Before calculating, say exactly what must be found or proved. Keep every restriction visible, because this is the kind of problem where a correct calculation can still answer the wrong question.

Editorial guidance: a common danger in a problem with this structure is this. Do not assume outcomes are equally likely until the random process has justified that sample space. A useful first hint from the textbook is: Label the six physical counters before conditioning on the colour. If you still need another nudge: How many red draw outcomes come from the all-red box? Now work through the complete solution in small steps. Pause whenever you want to reproduce a diagram, calculation or proof sentence in your notebook. Step 1.

Label the individual counters RR₁, RR₂ in the all-red box; RB-red, RB-blue in the mixed box; and BB₁, BB₂ in the all-blue box. Each physical counter is the observed draw with probability (1/3)(1/2) = 1/6. Step 2. Conditioning on a red draw leaves exactly three equally likely possibilities: RR₁, RR₂ and RB-red. The first two have a red companion, while the third has a blue companion. Step 3. The required probability is therefore 2/3.

Treating the two possible boxes as equally likely after seeing red would be incorrect: the all-red box has twice as many red draw outcomes as the mixed box. The textbook answer is: 2/3. Return to the original problem. title: A shortest route that must touch a line

chunks.text: Here is the problem. A path goes from A = (0, 2) to a point P on the line y = 0, then to B = (6, 4). Find the point P that gives the shortest total path, and prove that no other choice of P gives a shorter path. Before calculating, say exactly what must be found or proved. Keep every restriction visible, because this is the kind of problem where a correct calculation can still answer the wrong question.

Editorial guidance: a common danger in a problem with this structure is this. Finding one promising example is not enough. Keep the proof of the bound separate from the construction that reaches it. A useful first hint from the textbook is: Reflect one endpoint across the line the route must touch. If you still need another nudge: When does a broken path have the same length as the straight segment between its endpoints? Now work through the complete solution in small steps.

Pause whenever you want to reproduce a diagram, calculation or proof sentence in your notebook. Step 1. Reflect A across y = 0 to A′ = (0, -2). Reflection fixes every point P on y = 0 and preserves distances, so PA = PA′ for every allowed P. Step 2. Therefore AP + PB = A′P + PB. By the triangle inequality, this is at least the straight-line distance A′B. Equality holds exactly when P lies on the segment from A′ to B. Step 3.

That segment rises from y = -2 to y = 4, a total rise of 6. It reaches y = 0 after 2/6 = 1/3 of the journey, so its x-coordinate there is 0 + (1/3)(6 - 0) = 2. Thus P = (2, 0), which is an allowed point and attains the lower bound. Step 4. The point P = (2, 0) is allowed and makes the reflected route a straight segment. Every other point on y = 0 makes that route bent and strictly longer, so this P is the unique minimum.

The textbook answer is: P = (2, 0). Return to the original problem. Check that every condition has been used, every counted case appears once, and any claimed maximum, minimum or guarantee has actually been proved rather than guessed from examples.

Here is the problem. Each of five people is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a knave, who always lies. Person 1 says, “Exactly one of us is a knave.” Person 2 says, “Exactly two of us are knaves.” Person 3 says, “Exactly three of us are knaves.” Person 4 says, “Exactly four of us are knaves.” Person 5 says, “Exactly five of us are knaves.” How many knaves are there? Before calculating, say exactly what must be found or proved.

Keep every restriction visible, because this is the kind of problem where a correct calculation can still answer the wrong question. Editorial guidance: a common danger in a problem with this structure is this. A long list can miss a case or count the same object twice. Define one outcome and explain why the cases are complete and non-overlapping. A useful first hint from the textbook is: How many of the five different totals can be correct at once?

If you still need another nudge: Check that the number of false statements agrees with the proposed number of knaves. Now work through the complete solution in small steps. Pause whenever you want to reproduce a diagram, calculation or proof sentence in your notebook. Step 1. The five claims assert five different totals, so at most one of them can be true. If the actual number of knaves is k with 1 ≤ k ≤ 5, exactly Person k’s claim is true. Step 2.

Thus for any possible k between 1 and 5 there must be exactly one truth-teller and four liars. The knave count must consequently be k = 4. Step 3. Check this assignment: Person 4 tells the true statement that there are four knaves, and Persons 1, 2, 3 and 5 each make a false statement. Every person’s behaviour matches the assigned type. Step 4. The remaining possible count k = 0 is impossible: all five claims would then be false, although all five people would be knights.

Hence the checked assignment is the unique solution. The textbook answer is: Four knaves; Person 4 is the sole knight. Return to the original problem. title: Recovering ages from anonymous pair sums

chunks.text: Here is the problem. Four children have different whole-number ages in years. Their six pair sums are 14, 16, 17, 18, 19 and 21. How old is the oldest child? Before calculating, say exactly what must be found or proved. Keep every restriction visible, because this is the kind of problem where a correct calculation can still answer the wrong question. Editorial guidance: a common danger in a problem with this structure is this. Finding one promising example is not enough.

Keep the proof of the bound separate from the construction that reaches it. A useful first hint from the textbook is: Sort the ages and identify which pairs must give the smallest two and largest two sums. If you still need another nudge: Only the order of a + d and b + c remains unknown. Check both possibilities. Now work through the complete solution in small steps. Pause whenever you want to reproduce a diagram, calculation or proof sentence in your notebook. Step 1.

Let the four ages in increasing order be a < b < c < d. The smallest pair sum is a + b = 14 and the largest is c + d = 21. The second-smallest is a + c = 16: it is smaller than a + d, b + c, b + d and c + d. Similarly, the second-largest is b + d = 19. Step 2. The remaining sums 17 and 18 must be a + d and b + c, in some order. This leaves just two cases, rather than assuming which anonymous sum belongs to which pair. Step 3.

If b + c = 18, then 2a = (a + b) + (a + c) - (b + c) = 14 + 16 - 18 = 12. Thus a = 6, b = 8, c = 10 and d = 21 - c = 11. The unused pair a + d is 17, as required. Step 4. If b + c = 17, the same equation gives 2a = 14 + 16 - 17 = 13, so a = 6.5, contrary to the whole-number condition. This case is impossible. Step 5. The valid ages have pair sums 14, 16, 17, 18, 19 and 21 exactly, and are all different.

The oldest child is therefore 11. The textbook answer is: 11 years. The ages are 6, 8, 10 and 11. Return to the original problem. Check that every condition has been used, every counted case appears once, and any claimed maximum, minimum or guarantee has actually been proved rather than guessed from examples.

Here is the problem. Five prime numbers form an arithmetic sequence with common difference 6: each is 6 more than the one before. What is the sum of the five primes? Before calculating, say exactly what must be found or proved. Keep every restriction visible, because this is the kind of problem where a correct calculation can still answer the wrong question. title: Which integers are differences of squares?

chunks.text: Here is the problem. How many of the whole numbers from 1 to 100 can be written as the difference of two square numbers? Zero counts as a square number: for example, 9 = 9 - 0 and 8 = 9 - 1. Before calculating, say exactly what must be found or proved. Every square is congruent to 0 or 1 modulo 4. A difference of two squares can therefore have remainder 0, 1 or 3 modulo 4, but never remainder 2. This proves that the 25 numbers congruent to 2 modulo 4 are impossible. Step 2. We must also show that every other number works. Every positive odd integer can be written 2k + 1 with k ≥ 0, and 2k + 1 = (k + 1)2 - k2. Step 3.

Every positive multiple of 4 can be written 4k with k ≥ 1, and 4k = (k + 1)2 - (k - 1)2. When k = 1 the second square is zero, which the question expressly permits. Step 4. Thus the representable integers are exactly the odd numbers and multiples of 4. These disjoint classes contribute 50 + 25 = 75 numbers between 1 and 100.
